title: HTTP and TLS
sub: Read, send and time web requests by hand with curl, and inspect the certificates behind https
goals: Read an HTTP request and response line by line and name the job of each header you meet
Fetch, filter and time any URL with curl, and choose the flags that make it safe in scripts
Follow a redirect chain and explain 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 by what they do to the method
Split one request's time into DNS, TCP, TLS, server wait and download with curl -w
Read a certificate with openssl and check how many days it has left
Practice against a web server you run yourself, then against the public internet

blocks.text: Almost every service you will touch speaks HTTP: web pages, JSON APIs, package registries, your router's admin page, the dashboard of your homelab. HTTP is a plain-text conversation on top of TCP, which makes it the easiest protocol to learn by typing it. In this chapter you will build a small web server of your own, talk to it with `curl` until every header makes sense, measure where the time goes in a request, and look inside the TLS certificates that turn `http` into `https`. You finish by writing `site-check`, a script that audits a list of sites.

Practice against **your own machine first**. A server on `127.0.0.1` cannot be rate limited, cannot ban you and never changes its answers while you learn. After that, `example.com` (reserved for documentation) and `api.github.com` (public, light use) are fine. Do not run load or `-P` parallel loops against sites you do not own, and never send other people's credentials anywhere.
HTTP in one picture

**HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a request/response protocol. A **client** opens a TCP connection to a server, sends one **request**, and reads one **response**. Each message is text with a fixed shape: a first line, then header lines, then a blank line, then an optional body. HTTP/1.1 is defined in RFC 9112 (semantics in RFC 9110).

blocks.code:
request (client to server)                     response (server to client)

   GET /data/ HTTP/1.1          ⟪c:request line⟫        HTTP/1.1 200 OK            ⟪c:status line⟫
   Host: localhost:8000         ⟪y:headers⟫             Content-Type: text/html    ⟪y:headers⟫
   User-Agent: curl/8.7.1                              Content-Length: 412
   Accept: */*                                         Date: Thu, 08 Oct 2026 ...
                                ⟪d:blank line ends⟫                                ⟪d:blank line ends⟫
   (body, for POST/PUT)         ⟪g:body⟫                <!DOCTYPE html> ...       ⟪g:body⟫

blocks.text: Three properties shape everything else:

items.text: **It is text.** Lines end in CRLF (`\r\n`). You can type a request into `nc` and a server will answer it, as you will do below.
**It is stateless.** The server treats each request on its own. Anything that feels like a session (login, shopping cart) is built from **cookies** or tokens that the client sends back every time.

**It rides on TCP.** Before the first request there is a name lookup and a three-way handshake, and for `https` a TLS handshake as well. That is why the first request to a site is slower than the second, and why `curl -w` timings (later in this chapter) are so informative.

blocks.text: HTTP/1.0 had no `Host` header, so one IP address could serve only one site. HTTP/1.1 made `Host: example.com` mandatory, which lets thousands of sites share one IP. The header is also the reason `curl http://93.184.216.34` can return a different page from `curl http://example.com`: the IP picks the machine, the `Host` header picks the site on it.
Explore how a request is assembled, and what a typical response looks like for each method, in the explorer below. Change the method and the path and watch the lines change.
Messages in detail

**Request line.** `METHOD target VERSION`. The target is usually a path plus query string (`/search?q=ports`). **Status line.** `VERSION code reason`. Programs read the three-digit code; the reason phrase is decoration.

**Headers** are `Name: value` lines. Names are case-insensitive (`Content-Type` equals `content-type`; HTTP/2 requires lowercase). A **body** needs framing so the reader knows where it ends: either `Content-Length: N` (exactly N bytes follow), or `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` (a series of size-prefixed chunks, used when the length is unknown in advance), or the server closes the connection.

**HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.** HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) keeps the same methods, headers and status codes but sends them as compressed binary frames, and multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) does the same over QUIC, which runs on UDP port 443 and folds TLS 1.3 into its own handshake. For your purposes the meaning of a request does not change, only how it travels. `curl -v` and `curl -w '%{http_version}'` tell you which one you got.
The anatomy of a URL
A **URL** names a resource and says how to reach it. Every part has a job, and a mistake in any of them gives a distinct failure.

blocks.code:
https://alice:s3cret@api.example.com:8443/v1/users/42?active=true&sort=name#profile
   └─┬─┘   └────┬─────┘ └──────┬──────┘ └─┬─┘└────┬─────┘ └──────────┬──────────┘ └──┬──┘
   scheme   userinfo        host         port   path                query         fragment
            (avoid)      (DNS lookup)  (default   (sent to the    (key=value pairs,   (never sent;
                                       80/443)    server)          sent to server)     browser only)

blocks.title: A URL broken into the parts curl uses

tokens.exp: scheme: which protocol, and the default port (https 443, http 80)
host: looked up in DNS, and sent as the Host header
port: overrides the default
path: which resource on that server
query string: parameters, separated by &

blocks.text: Two rules save a lot of confusion. First, the **fragment** (`#profile`) is for the browser and is never sent in the request. Second, characters outside a small safe set must be **percent-encoded**: a space is `%20`, `&` is `%26`, `+` is `%2B`. If your data contains `&` or `=`, putting it raw in a query string changes its meaning. `curl --data-urlencode` does the encoding for you.

In zsh an unquoted `?` is a glob character, so `curl localhost:8001/hello?x=1` fails with `zsh: no matches found` before curl even starts. **Always quote URLs that contain `?`, `&`, `*`, `[` or `#`**: `curl 'localhost:8001/hello?x=1&y=2'`. An unquoted `&` also sends the command to the background and cuts the URL in half.
Your own web server

Python ships a static file server. It is the quickest way to get a real HTTP server whose every line you can watch, which is exactly what a learner needs. Run it in one Terminal tab, and use a second tab for `curl`.

blocks.name: python3 -m http.server
blocks.sum: Serve the files in a directory over HTTP so you can browse them or fetch them with curl.

how.text: The `http.server` module in Python's standard library listens on a TCP port (default 8000), accepts connections and answers `GET` and `HEAD` requests by mapping the URL path to a file under the directory. A path that is a directory returns an `index.html` if there is one, otherwise an auto-generated listing. It writes one log line per request to stderr, so the Terminal tab running it is a live access log.

It is a teaching tool, not a production server: no TLS, no authentication, one request handled per thread, and it will happily list every file in the folder you gave it. It answers with `HTTP/1.0` by default and closes the connection after each response.

flags.d: Bind to one address. Use `127.0.0.1` so only your own machine can connect; the default listens on every interface.
Serve this directory instead of the current one.
A positional number such as `8080`. Ports below 1024 are privileged on most systems.
Speak HTTP/1.1 and keep connections alive (`--protocol`, Python 3.11 and later).

examples.desc: Serve the practice lab on your own machine only
Serve another folder on all interfaces, for a phone or a second computer on your LAN
From a second tab, list the files the server exposes, one per line

gotchas: Without `--bind 127.0.0.1` every machine on your network can read the folder, and macOS shows the dialog "Do you want the application Python to accept incoming network connections?". Click Deny unless you meant to share it.
`Address already in use` means another process owns the port. Find it with `lsof -nP -iTCP:8000 -sTCP:LISTEN`, or pick another port.

blocks.text: Start it, then fetch from the second tab:

Each log line reads: client IP, two unused identity fields (`- -`), timestamp, the request line in quotes, the status code, and the body size (`-` when not recorded). It is the same shape as the lines in `access.log`.

For tests that need more than static files, create `echo.py` in `~/lab`. It is a 50-line server that reports back exactly what it received, and it can also produce redirects, status codes, cookies and delays on demand. Run it in its own tab with `python3 echo.py`.
You will write servers properly in [Python for networking](#py-net). For now it is a target that behaves the same every time.
curl, the HTTP workbench

`curl` transfers data to or from a URL using HTTP, HTTPS, FTP and many other protocols. It ships with macOS, so every example here works on a fresh Mac. [Network basics](#networks) introduced `curl -v`; this card is the working reference.

blocks.name: curl
blocks.sum: Send an HTTP request from the command line and print the response, headers, timings or exit status.

how.text: `curl` is a command-line front end to libcurl. It resolves the host, opens a TCP connection, runs a TLS handshake for `https`, sends one request and writes the **response body to stdout**. Everything else it wants to tell you (progress meter, errors, `-v` diagnostics) goes to **stderr**, so you can pipe the body onward while still seeing problems.

By default curl does not treat HTTP errors as failures: a `404` page is a successful transfer and exit status `0`. For scripts, add `-f` or read the code with `-w '%{http_code}'`. Redirects are shown, not followed, until you add `-L`.
Options can be combined (`-sSL`). Order does not matter except for options that take a value (`-o file`, `-H header`), where the value must follow directly.

gotchas: Exit status `0` does not mean the page is good. Without `-f` a `404` or `503` still exits `0`. Check `%{http_code}` or use `-f`.
`curl -v | grep` finds nothing, because `-v` writes to stderr. Use `2>&1`, and add `-o /dev/null` so the body does not flood the output.
`-k` turns off the check that you are talking to the real server. A man-in-the-middle passes it silently. Use it to confirm "the only problem is the certificate", then fix the certificate.
Credentials in a URL or in `-u user:pass` appear in `ps` output and your shell history. For real secrets read the value from a file or prompt (`-u user` asks for the password).
notes: Exact text of the `*` lines in `-v` depends on the curl version and TLS library. macOS 12 shipped curl 7.79; current releases ship 8.x, which adds options such as `--json` (7.82) and `%header{name}` (7.84). Check yours with `curl --version`.

blocks.text: Reading a verbose transcript
Run `-v` against your practice server and label every line. The three prefixes are the whole key: `*` is curl talking about itself, `>` is what it **sent**, `<` is what it **received**.

blocks.code:
$ curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8001/status/404
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:8001...
* Connected to 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) port 8001
> GET /status/404 HTTP/1.1
> Host: 127.0.0.1:8001
> User-Agent: curl/8.7.1
> Accept: */*
>
* HTTP 1.0, assume close after body
< HTTP/1.0 404 Not Found
< Server: BaseHTTP/0.6 Python/3.13.1
< Date: Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:44:51 GMT
< Content-Type: application/json
< Content-Length: 15
<
* Closing connection
{"status": 404}

blocks.text: The `>` block is the request your Mac built: a request line, `Host` (derived from the URL), `User-Agent` (curl names itself) and `Accept: */*` (any content type is fine). The blank `>` line ends the headers. The `<` block is the answer: a status line, then headers describing the body, then the body itself on stdout. Look at `HTTP 1.0, assume close after body`: because `http.server` replies with HTTP/1.0, curl knows the server will close the connection when it is done.

Start `echo.py` in one tab. In another, run `curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8001/` and find, in order: the line that proves the TCP connection opened, the request line, the `Host` header, the status line, and the `Content-Length` of the reply. Then run it with `-H 'X-Demo: yes'` and find your header in the JSON the server sends back.
Against a public site the same command first shows a TLS handshake. Here is the shape of it, abridged:

blocks.code:
$ curl -sv -o /dev/null https://example.com
* Host example.com:443 was resolved.
*   Trying 93.184.216.34:443...
* Connected to example.com (93.184.216.34) port 443
* ALPN: curl offers h2,http/1.1
* (304) (OUT), TLS handshake, Client hello (1):
* (304) (IN), TLS handshake, Server hello (2):
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / AEAD-CHACHA20-POLY1305-SHA256
* Server certificate:
*  subject: CN=www.example.org
*  start date: Jan 30 00:00:00 2026 GMT
*  expire date: Mar  1 23:59:59 2027 GMT
*  issuer: C=US; O=DigiCert Inc; CN=DigiCert Global G3 TLS ECC SHA384 2020 CA1
*  SSL certificate verify ok.
* using HTTP/2
> GET / HTTP/2
> Host: example.com
< HTTP/2 200
< content-type: text/html

blocks.title: Your transcript will not match line for line

blocks.text: Apple's curl may be built against a different TLS library than the one Homebrew installs, and each prints these `*` lines in its own wording (`(304) (OUT)` is the Apple build; OpenSSL builds print `TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Client hello (1):`). The `>` and `<` lines are protocol text and never change.
Methods, idempotency and status codes

The **method** says what the client wants done with the resource. Two properties matter for scripts and retries. A method is **safe** if it only reads. A method is **idempotent** if sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once, which decides whether a client may retry automatically after a timeout.

head: Method
Typical use
Safe
Idempotent
Body in request
rows: create something, submit a form, run an action

blocks.text: The **status code** is the server's verdict, and the first digit is the class. Learn the classes cold and look up the individual codes as you meet them.

head: Class
Meaning
Codes you will see most
rows: `200 OK`, `201 Created`, `204 No Content`, `206 Partial Content`
go elsewhere or use your cache
`400 Bad Request`, `401 Unauthorized`, `403 Forbidden`, `404 Not Found`, `405 Method Not Allowed`, `408`, `409 Conflict`, `418`, `429 Too Many Requests`
`500 Internal Server Error`, `502 Bad Gateway`, `503 Service Unavailable`, `504 Gateway Timeout`

blocks.text: Two pairs are confused constantly. **401** means "I do not know who you are" (missing or bad credentials) and **403** means "I know who you are and the answer is no". **502** and **504** come from a proxy or load balancer in front of the real application: 502 means the upstream sent garbage or refused the connection, 504 means it took too long.
Use your echo server to see each class on demand:
Headers that matter
Headers carry metadata in both directions. You do not need to memorize hundreds, only the ones that explain real behavior.

head: Header
Direction
What it does
rows: which site on this IP; required in HTTP/1.1
names the client; some servers answer differently to `curl`
content types the client can handle (`application/json`)
compression the client understands (`gzip, br`); `curl --compressed` sets it
size of the body in bytes
where to go next, with a 3xx status
asks the client to store a cookie
version markers a client can send back to ask "has it changed?"
conditional GET; the server may answer `304` with no body
software name; handy for fingerprinting your own servers
tells browsers to use only https for this host for a period

blocks.text: Content negotiation

The client states preferences and the server picks. `Accept` selects the format, `Accept-Language` the language, `Accept-Encoding` the compression. Try it on an API: `curl -H 'Accept: application/json' ...`. If the server cannot satisfy it you may get `406 Not Acceptable` or just its default. Compression is invisible in a browser, which always asks for it. curl sends no `Accept-Encoding` unless you add `--compressed`, in which case it also decompresses the reply for you.
Cookies

A server asks the client to remember a value with `Set-Cookie`; a cookie-aware client returns it in `Cookie` on later requests to the same site. curl keeps no cookies unless you give it a **cookie jar**: `-c file` writes cookies the server sets, `-b file` sends them.

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -c jar.txt http://127.0.0.1:8001/login -o /dev/null
$ tail -1 jar.txt
#HttpOnly_127.0.0.1	FALSE	/	FALSE	0	session	abc123
$ curl -s -b jar.txt http://127.0.0.1:8001/ | grep -i cookie
    "Cookie": "session=abc123"

blocks.text: The attributes on a cookie are security controls: `HttpOnly` hides it from page scripts, `Secure` limits it to https, `SameSite` limits cross-site sending, and `Max-Age` or `Expires` sets its lifetime. A cookie without an expiry (the `0` in the jar) is a **session cookie** that dies when the browser closes.
Caching and conditional requests

A response may be reused without asking again until it expires (`Cache-Control: max-age=...`). After that the client can **revalidate**: it sends the version marker it saved, and if nothing changed the server answers `304 Not Modified` with no body, saving the transfer. Python's file server supports `Last-Modified`, so you can watch the exchange:

blocks.code:
$ curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8000/README.txt | grep -i last-modified
Last-Modified: Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:12:03 GMT
$ curl -sI -H 'If-Modified-Since: Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:12:03 GMT' http://127.0.0.1:8000/README.txt | head -1
HTTP/1.0 304 Not Modified

blocks.text: Redirects
A 3xx response with a `Location` header tells the client to ask somewhere else. The code states **how permanent** the move is and **what happens to the method**.

head: Code
Meaning
Method on the next request
rows: the URL has a new home forever; caches may remember
clients may change POST to GET
clients usually change POST to GET
go and GET a result page (after a form post)

blocks.text: The `301`/`302` ambiguity is historical: early browsers rewrote POST into GET, so the standard added 307 and 308 to say "keep the method" unambiguously. Your echo server has a two-hop chain, `/old` to `/new` to `/`. Without `-L` curl shows only the first hop. With `-L` it follows both:

blocks.code:
$ curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8001/old | head -3
HTTP/1.0 301 Moved Permanently
Server: BaseHTTP/0.6 Python/3.13.1
Date: Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:50:11 GMT
$ curl -sIL http://127.0.0.1:8001/old | grep -E '^(HTTP|Location)'
HTTP/1.0 301 Moved Permanently
Location: /new
HTTP/1.0 302 Found
Location: /
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
$ curl -sL -o /dev/null -w '%{num_redirects} hops, ended at %{url_effective} with %{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8001/old
2 hops, ended at http://127.0.0.1:8001/ with 200

blocks.text: Python's file server also redirects: asking for a directory without the trailing slash (`/data`) gets a `301` to `/data/`. Real sites redirect `http` to `https` and the bare domain to `www`, so the chain of a public site is worth printing once:

blocks.code:
$ curl -sI http://example.com
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 209
Server: ECAcc (dcd/7D2B)
Date: Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:41:00 GMT
Cache-Control: max-age=604800

$ curl -sI http://example.com/missing | head -1
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
$ curl -s http://example.com | head -4
<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Example Domain</title>

blocks.text: `curl -L -d 'a=1' URL` follows a `301`, `302` or `303` with a **GET** and drops the body, matching browser behavior. Use `--post301`/`--post302` to force POST again, or fix the server to answer `307`/`308`. By default curl also drops your `Authorization` header when a redirect leads to a different host, so credentials are not leaked; `--location-trusted` turns that protection off, so avoid it.
Timing a request with -w

`-w` (`--write-out`) tells curl to print a format string after the transfer, with `%{variable}` placeholders filled from the transfer's measurements. It turns curl into a stopwatch. All `time_*` values are **cumulative seconds since the start**, so a phase's duration is the difference between two of them.

blocks.name: curl -w
blocks.sum: Print selected facts about a finished transfer, such as the status code, timings and sizes, using a format string.

how.text: After curl finishes, it replaces each `%{name}` in the format string with that fact and prints the result to stdout. Escapes `\n`, `\t` and `\r` work inside the string. Use `-o /dev/null -s` to suppress the body and meter, so the line is the only output.

The `time_*` variables mark moments on one clock that starts when curl begins. In order: `time_namelookup` (DNS finished), `time_connect` (TCP established), `time_appconnect` (TLS finished; `0` for plain http), `time_pretransfer` (ready to send the request), `time_starttransfer` (first byte of the response arrived), `time_total` (everything done). Subtract neighbors to get the cost of one phase.

flags.d: The final response status code (`000` if no response arrived).
Seconds until the name was resolved.
Seconds until the TCP handshake completed.
Seconds until the TLS handshake completed (0 for http).
Seconds until the first response byte (time to first byte).
Total seconds for the whole transfer.
Seconds spent in the redirect hops before the final request.
Body bytes received.
Average download speed in bytes per second.
The final URL after redirects.
How many redirects were followed.
The server IP actually used.
The response `Content-Type`.

examples.desc: A one-line status and timing report
Keep a reusable format in a file and load it with @
Turn the timings into milliseconds for each phase
examples.code: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_appconnect} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}\n' {{url}} | awk '{printf "dns %.0f  tcp %.0f  tls %.0f  wait %.0f  download %.0f (ms)\n", $1*1000, ($2-$1)*1000, ($3-$2)*1000, ($4-$3)*1000, ($5-$4)*1000}'

examples.desc: Median total time over five requests
examples.code: for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}\n' {{url}}; done | sort -n | sed -n 3p

anat.exp: print the status and total time after the transfer

gotchas: For plain `http`, `time_appconnect` is `0`, so subtracting it gives nonsense. Use `https` for the per-phase awk above, or compute TLS only when the value is non-zero.
`%{http_code}` shows the last response after `-L`. Add `-w '%{num_redirects}'` to know whether you were redirected at all.
notes: `%{json}` (curl 7.70 and later) prints every variable as one JSON object, which pipes straight into `jq`.

blocks.text: Read the phases as a timeline. The whole point is to put a number on "the site is slow" and say which part is slow:

blocks.code:
0 ms                                                                         total
  │ DNS  │  TCP connect  │   TLS handshake    │ request │   server wait   │ download│
  ├──────┼───────────────┼────────────────────┼─────────┼─────────────────┼─────────┤
  │      │               │                    │         │                 │         │
  ▼      ▼               ▼                    ▼         ▼                 ▼         ▼
 start  ⟪c:namelookup⟫    ⟪g:connect⟫            ⟪y:appconnect⟫  ⟪m:pretransfer⟫   ⟪r:starttransfer⟫  ⟪w:total⟫

   DNS slow            -> resolver or network problem   (see the DNS chapter)
   connect slow        -> distance, packet loss, or a firewall dropping SYN
   appconnect - connect -> TLS cost: certificate chain, CPU, or an old protocol
   starttransfer - pretransfer -> the server is thinking: application or database
   total - starttransfer -> the body is big, or the link is slow

blocks.text: Save a reusable format file so you can reuse it everywhere. Note that in a `-w @file` the text is literal, including newlines.

blocks.code:
status: %{http_code}  (HTTP/%{http_version})
          ip: %{remote_ip}
         dns: %{time_namelookup}s
         tcp: %{time_connect}s
         tls: %{time_appconnect}s
  first byte: %{time_starttransfer}s
       total: %{time_total}s
        size: %{size_download} bytes

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w @curl-format.txt https://example.com
      status: 200  (HTTP/2)
          ip: 93.184.216.34
         dns: 0.012418s
         tcp: 0.031207s
         tls: 0.095820s
  first byte: 0.142561s
       total: 0.143004s
        size: 1256 bytes

blocks.text: Here DNS cost 12 ms, TCP 19 ms (0.0312 minus 0.0124), TLS 65 ms, and the server needed 47 ms after the handshake. Run the same command a second time to see what caching in your resolver does to `dns`. For a test where the time is large on purpose, use `/delay/1` on the echo server: `time_starttransfer` jumps to about 1 second while `time_connect` stays near zero, which is the signature of a slow application on a fast network.
Sending data: forms, JSON, files, credentials
A request body needs a `Content-Type` that tells the server how to parse it. curl picks one for `-d` and `-F`, and you override it with `-H`.

blocks.name: curl -d
blocks.sum: Send a request body: form fields, JSON, a file upload, or credentials, with the right method and headers.
blocks.syntax: curl [-X METHOD] [-d data | --data-urlencode data | -F field=value | -T file] [-H header] [-u user[:pass]] URL

how.text: `-d` sends its argument as the body and switches the method to POST. The default content type is `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, which expects `key=value&key2=value2`. For JSON you must set `Content-Type: application/json` yourself; curl does not guess.

`--data-urlencode` percent-encodes the value so characters such as `&`, `=`, `+` and spaces survive. With `-G` the pairs go onto the query string of a GET instead of the body. `-F` builds a `multipart/form-data` body, which is how browsers upload files; `-F 'file=@photo.jpg'` reads the file. `-T file` does a raw `PUT` of the file as the body.

`-u user:pass` sends HTTP Basic authentication: the header `Authorization: Basic base64(user:pass)`. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption; anyone who sees the header can read the password, which is why Basic must only travel over https.

flags.d: Send DATA as the body with POST. `-d @file` reads it from a file; `-d @-` reads stdin.
Like `-d` but URL-encodes the value (`name=value` or `name@file`).
Move `-d` data to the query string and use GET.
Add a multipart form field; `name=@path` uploads a file.
Upload FILE with PUT.
Set the method word (`PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`). It does not add a body.
Set a header such as `Content-Type: application/json` or `Authorization: Bearer TOKEN`.
HTTP Basic credentials. Omit `:PASS` to be prompted.
Send cookies from FILE / save received cookies to FILE.
Shorthand for `-d` plus JSON `Content-Type` and `Accept` headers (curl 7.82 and later).

Post JSON
Build a query string safely, with GET
Upload a file as multipart form data

the body, which also makes the method POST

gotchas: Forgetting the `Content-Type` header on a JSON post is the classic cause of `400` and `415 Unsupported Media Type`: the server is parsing your JSON as a form.
`-d` with a file via `@file` strips newlines. Use `--data-binary @file` to send the file byte for byte.
`-X POST` together with `-d` is redundant, and `-X GET` with `-d` can break redirects. Let curl choose the method unless you need `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`.

blocks.text: The echo server shows what arrived, which is the fastest way to catch a mistake. This is real output from a form post:
Note `Content-Length: 21`, the exact byte count of the body, and the form content type that curl added without being asked.
TLS and certificates

**TLS** (Transport Layer Security) wraps a TCP connection so that nobody on the path can read or alter the traffic, and so that the client can verify which server it reached. `https` is HTTP inside TLS. The handshake in TLS 1.3 takes one round trip:

blocks.code:
client                                                          server
     │ ── ClientHello: versions, ciphers, key share, ⟪c:SNI = example.com⟫, ALPN ─▶ │
     │                                                                              │
     │ ◀─ ServerHello (chosen cipher, key share) ───────────────────────────────── │
     │ ◀─ ⟪y:Certificate chain⟫ + signature proving it owns the key ───────────────── │
     │ ◀─ Finished ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
     │ ── Finished ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶ │
     │ ══════════════ ⟪g:encrypted HTTP request and response⟫ ═══════════════════════ │

blocks.text: The **SNI** (Server Name Indication) extension sends the hostname in clear text so the server can pick the right certificate when many sites share one IP. **ALPN** negotiates the application protocol in the same message, which is how `h2` (HTTP/2) is agreed. The key exchange produces a shared secret that no observer can derive, and everything after the handshake is encrypted.
What a certificate proves

A **certificate** binds a public key to one or more names, and is signed by a **certificate authority** (CA). The server sends a chain: its own (leaf) certificate, then intermediates. Your Mac trusts a set of root CAs in the system keychain, and a certificate is accepted only when all of these hold:

items.text: The chain leads to a trusted root, and each signature verifies.
The hostname you asked for matches a name in the certificate's **Subject Alternative Name** list. The old `CN` field is not used for this.
The server proves it holds the private key (the signature in the handshake).

blocks.text: When one fails, curl stops with exit status `60` ("SSL certificate problem") and a reason such as `certificate has expired`, `self-signed certificate`, or `unable to get local issuer certificate`. Exit `35` means the handshake itself failed.

blocks.name: openssl s_client
blocks.sum: Open a TLS connection to a host and port, print the handshake and the certificate chain it received.

how.text: `s_client` is a bare TLS client: it connects, performs the handshake, prints the negotiated protocol, cipher and the server's certificate chain, then waits for you to type. Redirect stdin from `/dev/null` so it exits right after the handshake. `-servername` sets the SNI; without it a server hosting many sites may return a default certificate for the wrong name, which is a common false alarm.

The output contains the leaf certificate as a PEM block between `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----` and `-----END CERTIFICATE-----`. Pipe that block to `openssl x509` to decode it. It works on any TLS service, not only web servers: mail on 993, LDAPS on 636, your own services.

flags.d: Where to connect.
Send NAME as SNI. Give the same name you would browse to.
Print every certificate in the chain, not only the leaf.
Offer only that protocol version; useful to test what a server still allows.
Start in plain text and upgrade (`smtp`, `imap`, `ftp`) for mail servers.

examples.desc: See the handshake summary
Check whether a server still accepts TLS 1.2
Decode the certificate that a server presents
Print only the expiry date
Exit status says whether the cert is still good in 30 days
examples.code: openssl s_client -connect {{host}}:443 -servername {{host}} < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -checkend 2592000 && echo "valid for 30+ days"

no input, so the session ends after the handshake
hide the handshake chatter on stderr
decode the PEM certificate that came out on stdout

gotchas: Without `< /dev/null` the command waits for input forever. Press Control-D to close it.
Handshake diagnostics go to stderr and the PEM block goes to stdout. That is why `2>/dev/null` before the second openssl keeps the pipe clean.
notes: macOS `/usr/bin/openssl` is LibreSSL, not OpenSSL. Basic `s_client` and `x509` work the same; some newer OpenSSL options are missing. `brew install openssl@3` installs the full one under `/opt/homebrew/opt/openssl@3/bin/openssl`.

blocks.name: openssl x509
blocks.sum: Read a PEM certificate from stdin or a file and print chosen fields: subject, issuer, validity dates, fingerprint.

how.text: `x509` parses one certificate and, with `-noout`, prints only what you ask for. Without `-in` it reads standard input, which is how it receives the output of `s_client`. `-dates` prints both `notBefore` and `notAfter`; `-enddate` prints only the latter, in the format `notAfter=Mar  1 23:59:59 2027 GMT`.

`-checkend N` asks "will this certificate still be valid N seconds from now?". It prints a sentence and sets the exit status: `0` if yes, `1` if it will have expired. That is the cleanest way to test expiry in a script, because it avoids parsing a date string.

flags.d: Do not print the certificate itself.
Who the certificate was issued to.
The CA that signed it.
`notBefore` and `notAfter`.
SHA-256 fingerprint of the certificate, to compare out of band.
Print everything in human-readable form, including Subject Alternative Names.
Exit 0 if the certificate is still valid after that many seconds, else 1.

examples.desc: Print the validity period of a certificate file
List the DNS names the certificate covers
examples.code: openssl s_client -connect {{host}}:443 -servername {{host}} < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep -A1 'Alternative Name' | tail -1 | tr ',' '\n' | sed 's/^ *//'

examples.desc: Print the SHA-256 fingerprint of a server's certificate

gotchas: The `notAfter` value is padded with two spaces for single-digit days (`Mar  1`), which matters if you split it with `awk`: use `-F=` and keep the rest of the line as one field, or avoid parsing and use `-checkend`.

blocks.code:
$ openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates
subject=CN=www.example.org
issuer=C=US, O=DigiCert Inc, CN=DigiCert Global G3 TLS ECC SHA384 2020 CA1
notBefore=Jan 30 00:00:00 2026 GMT
notAfter=Mar  1 23:59:59 2027 GMT

blocks.text: `curl -k` and similar "ignore certificate errors" switches remove the only proof that you are talking to the real server. Use them for a few seconds to learn that the certificate is the sole problem, such as a homelab service with a self-signed certificate, then fix it: install a proper certificate, or tell curl to trust that one CA with `--cacert ca.pem`. Never leave `-k` in a script that sends passwords or tokens.
Other clients and raw HTTP
`curl` is not the only tool, and it helps to know three more.

blocks.name: wget
blocks.sum: Download files over HTTP, HTTPS or FTP, with automatic retry and resume; strong at recursive mirroring.

how.text: `wget` is built for downloads that must survive a bad connection: it retries by default, resumes with `-c`, and can follow links to mirror a site. By default it saves the body to a file named after the URL; curl writes to the terminal. macOS does not include it, so install it with Homebrew.

flags.d: Save to FILE. `-O -` writes to stdout, like curl.
Continue a partial download.
Quiet.
Check that a URL exists without downloading it.
Print the server's response headers.
Add a request header.

Stream a page to stdout and count its lines
Check a list of URLs without downloading them
examples.code: xargs -n 1 wget -q --spider < urls.txt && echo "all URLs exist"

gotchas: `wget` prints its progress to stderr and saves to a file, so `wget URL | grep x` finds nothing. Add `-qO-` to pipe the body.

blocks.name: http
blocks.sum: A friendlier HTTP client (HTTPie) with colored output, JSON by default and a compact syntax for headers, fields and queries.

how.text: HTTPie prints the request and response in a readable, highlighted layout and treats `key=value` items as JSON string fields, `key:=123` as raw JSON (numbers, booleans), `Header:value` as headers and `key==value` as query parameters. When stdout is not a terminal (a pipe or a file) it prints only the body with no color, so it behaves in pipelines.

Print only the response body.

blocks.text: Speaking HTTP by hand with nc

Because HTTP is text, a generic TCP tool can be a web client. `nc` (netcat) opens a socket and moves bytes; you supply the request. `printf` writes the exact bytes including the CRLF line endings, and `Connection: close` asks the server to hang up after replying so `nc` exits.

blocks.code:
$ printf 'GET /README.txt HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' | nc 127.0.0.1 8000
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Server: SimpleHTTP/0.6 Python/3.13.1
Date: Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:58:30 GMT
Content-type: text/plain
Content-Length: 214
Last-Modified: Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:12:03 GMT

Welcome to the lab ...

blocks.text:
The ending matters: the final `
` of `

` at the end of the request is the blank line that finishes the headers. Leave it out and the server waits for more. [Ports and Scanning](#ports) covers `nc` in depth.
Pipe recipes
This is where the output of one command becomes the input of the next. Each recipe below is a pattern you will reuse.
**JSON API to a table.** `curl` fetches, `jq` shapes. `-r` prints raw strings without quotes, so `@tsv` output lines up for `column`.

blocks.code:
$ curl -s https://api.github.com/users/octocat | jq -r '[.login, .public_repos, .followers] | @tsv'
octocat	8	21540
$ curl -s 'https://api.github.com/repos/python/cpython' | jq -r '"\(.full_name) is written mostly in \(.language)"'
python/cpython is written mostly in Python

blocks.text: **Headers to key/value pairs.** HTTP header lines end in `\r`, which breaks `awk` and `jq` unless you strip it first:

blocks.code: curl -sI {{url}} | tr -d '\r' | awk -F': ' 'NR > 1 && NF >= 2 {print tolower($1) "=" $2}'

blocks.text: **Headers as JSON**, using `jq` to build an object from the lines:

blocks.code: curl -sI {{url}} | tr -d '\r' | jq -Rn '[inputs | select(test("^[^:]+: ")) | capture("^(?<k>[^:]+): (?<v>.*)$") | {(.k | ascii_downcase): .v}] | add'

blocks.text: **Check many URLs in parallel.** Build the URLs, feed them to `xargs`, and let each curl print one self-describing line. `-P 4` runs four at a time, so it finishes faster; keep it small and only use it on your own sites.

blocks.code: sed 's|^|https://|' hosts.txt | xargs -P 4 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 10 -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s {}\n' {}

blocks.text: The `{}` in the format string is replaced by `xargs` with the URL, and the output lines can arrive in any order, so `| sort -k3` afterward. Against your lab, with the simulator:

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ for h in $(head -3 hosts.txt); do echo "$h $(curl -sI http://$h | head -1)"; done
example.com HTTP/1.1 200 OK
python.org HTTP/1.1 200 OK
github.com HTTP/1.1 200 OK

tokens.exp: turn bare domains into URLs, one per line
hand each line to another command as an argument
run four curls at the same time
the placeholder {} stands for each input line
quiet, discard each body
never wait more than 10 seconds
print status, time and the URL
the URL goes here, as curl's argument

blocks.text: **Download and verify a checksum.** Never run or install a download whose hash you have not checked against a source you trust:

blocks.code:
curl -fLO {{url}}/tool.tar.gz
curl -fsSL {{url}}/tool.tar.gz.sha256 -o tool.sha256
shasum -a 256 -c tool.sha256

blocks.text: **Print a redirect chain.** `-I` with `-L` prints the headers of every hop, and `grep` keeps the lines that tell the story:

blocks.code: curl -sIL http://github.com | tr -d '\r' | grep -iE '^(HTTP|location):'

blocks.text: **Status code as a number in a script.**

blocks.code:
code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 10 {{url}})
[[ $code == 2* ]] && echo "up ($code)" || echo "problem ($code)"

blocks.text: `2*` inside `[[ ]]` is a pattern match, so any `2xx` passes.
**Wait for your own server to come up**, a common need when scripting a dev server:

blocks.code: until curl -sf -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8001/; do sleep 1; done; echo ready

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Unquoted `?` or `&` in a URL.** zsh reports `no matches found` or backgrounds the command. Quote the URL.
**Trusting exit status `0`.** curl succeeded at transferring a 500 page. Use `-f` or `%{http_code}`.
**JSON without a content type.** The server sees a form. Add `-H 'Content-Type: application/json'`.
**Comparing `https` and `http` timings.** `time_appconnect` is `0` on plain http, so phase arithmetic breaks.
**Testing the wrong host.** `curl http://IP` sends `Host: IP`. To test a site on a specific server use `--resolve` or `-H 'Host: name'`.
**`-k` left in a script.** It silently disables the security that TLS exists to provide.
**Hammering a public API.** Unauthenticated GitHub allows about 60 requests an hour per IP. A loop will hit `403` with an `x-ratelimit-remaining: 0` header, and that header is worth reading.

blocks.text: Practice
Start `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1` in `~/lab` in one tab, and `python3 echo.py` in a second, then work from a third.

blocks.title: Serve and inspect

task.text: With the file server running in `~/lab`, fetch `README.txt` from it with curl and save it as `readme-copy.txt`. Then compare it with the original and look at the server tab to find the log line your request produced.

hints: Use `-o` to name the output file.
`diff` prints nothing when two files are identical.
blocks.solution:
curl -s -o readme-copy.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/README.txt
diff README.txt readme-copy.txt && echo identical

why.text: The server maps the URL path to a file under the directory and returns the bytes unchanged. The server tab shows `"GET /README.txt HTTP/1.1" 200 -`, the same shape as a line from `access.log`.

blocks.verify: [[ -s readme-copy.txt ]] && diff -q README.txt readme-copy.txt > /dev/null && echo OK

blocks.title: Only the status

task.text: Print only the three-digit status code of `http://127.0.0.1:8001/status/418`, with nothing else on the line, and then make a one-line command that exits with status `22` when the code is 4xx or 5xx.

hints: The flag that turns HTTP errors into curl failures is `-f`.

why.text: Without `-f` curl reports success for any response it could read. With `-f` it exits `22` on codes of 400 and above. Scripts choose between the two depending on whether they need the code (use `-w`) or only a pass/fail (use `-f`).

blocks.title: Walk the redirect chain

task.text: `http://127.0.0.1:8001/old` redirects twice. Print each hop's status line and `Location`, then print one line with the number of hops and the final URL.

hints: `-I` shows headers; adding `-L` follows redirects and prints headers for every hop.
blocks.solution:
curl -sIL http://127.0.0.1:8001/old | tr -d '\r' | grep -E '^(HTTP|Location)'
curl -sL -o /dev/null -w '%{num_redirects} hops, ends at %{url_effective}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8001/old

why.text: Without `-L` you see only the first 301. Following redirects is a client choice; the server only says where to go next. `tr -d '\r'` removes the carriage returns that would confuse later tools.

blocks.title: Where does the time go?

task.text: For `https://example.com`, print how many milliseconds were spent on DNS, TCP connect, TLS handshake and waiting for the first byte, one line, using a single curl and a single awk. Then run it three times and note which phase varies most.

hints: The `time_*` values are cumulative since the start, so subtract neighbors.
blocks.solution: curl -so /dev/null -w '%{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_appconnect} %{time_starttransfer}\n' https://example.com | awk '{printf "dns %.0f  tcp %.0f  tls %.0f  wait %.0f (ms)\n", $1*1000, ($2-$1)*1000, ($3-$2)*1000, ($4-$3)*1000}'

why.text: Each value is a timestamp, not a duration. DNS usually changes the most between runs (cache hit versus miss); TCP connect follows your distance to the server; TLS costs roughly one more round trip.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose, then fix it

task.text: Run each of these, read the error, and fix it:

items.text: `curl -d '{"a":1}' http://127.0.0.1:8001/api | jq -r '.headers["Content-Type"]'` shows a form content type, but the server must see JSON.
`curl -sf http://127.0.0.1:8001/delay/5 --max-time 1; echo $?` and explain the status.

hints: The first one fails in zsh before curl starts. Which characters did zsh expand or treat specially?
For the second, curl cannot guess JSON; you must say so with a header.
Look up exit code 28 in the `curl` card.
blocks.solution:
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/status/404?x=1&y=2'
curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"a":1}' http://127.0.0.1:8001/api | jq -r '.headers["Content-Type"]'
curl -sf --max-time 1 http://127.0.0.1:8001/delay/5; echo $?

why.text: Quoting stops zsh from treating `?` as a glob and `&` as "run in background". The JSON post needs an explicit `Content-Type`. The last command prints `28`, the curl exit status for "operation timed out", because the server was slower than `--max-time`.

blocks.title: How long has this certificate got?

task.text: Print the `notAfter` date of the certificate served by `example.com`, then write one line that prints `OK` if it is still valid in 30 days and `RENEW SOON` if not.

hints: Pipe `openssl s_client` to `openssl x509`. Send `< /dev/null` to `s_client`.
blocks.solution:
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -checkend 2592000 > /dev/null && echo OK || echo "RENEW SOON"

why.text: `-checkend` sets the exit status, so `&&` and `||` can act on it without parsing any date strings.

questions.q: A request to a URL returns `404` and `curl` exits with status 0. Which flag makes curl exit non-zero for that response?
questions.why: `-f` (`--fail`) treats HTTP codes of 400 and above as failures and exits 22. Without it a 404 page is just a successfully downloaded document.

questions.q: You see `> Host: example.com` in `curl -v` output. What does the `>` mean?

options.text: curl received this line from the server
curl sent this line to the server
curl is describing its own state
the line was redirected to a file

questions.why: `>` marks request lines curl sent, `<` marks response lines it received, and `*` is curl's own commentary.

questions.q: Which response means "the move is permanent and the client must repeat the same method and body"?
questions.why: `308 Permanent Redirect` keeps the method. `301` may be turned into a GET by clients, `302` is temporary, and `303` always switches to GET.

questions.q: A `-w` report shows `time_connect=0.040` and `time_appconnect=0.115`. How long did the TLS handshake take, in milliseconds?
questions.why: The values are cumulative, so TLS took `time_appconnect - time_connect = 0.075` seconds, or 75 ms.

questions.q: Why does `curl -v https://host/path | grep Host` print nothing?

options.text: the verbose lines go to stderr, not stdout

questions.why: `-v` writes diagnostics to stderr. Use `2>&1` to merge them into the pipe, and `-o /dev/null` to discard the body.

questions.q: Which command tells you whether a server's certificate stays valid for another 30 days without parsing dates?
questions.why: `-checkend N` exits 0 when the certificate will still be valid in N seconds, and 1 when it will not.

blocks.text: Build `site-check.zsh`: it reads a file of URLs and prints one line per site with the HTTP status, the total time, and for https sites the certificate expiry. It uses everything in the chapter and teaches the pattern of "one function that checks one thing, a loop that applies it to a list".
Step 1: One URL, by hand
Prove that every piece works on a single site before you script it:

blocks.code:
curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 10 -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' {{url}}
openssl s_client -connect {{host}}:443 -servername {{host}} < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate

blocks.text: Step 2: The URL list
Create `urls.txt`. Lines starting with `#` are comments and blank lines are skipped.

blocks.code:
# my sites
http://127.0.0.1:8000/
http://127.0.0.1:8001/status/503
https://example.com
https://api.github.com

blocks.text: Step 3: The script
`check_one` turns a URL into one output line. Failures are data, not crashes: if curl cannot connect the code is `000`, and a missing certificate prints `-`.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# Usage: ./site-check.zsh urls.txt
# Prints: URL, HTTP status, total seconds, certificate expiry.
setopt pipefail

file=${1:?usage: site-check.zsh URLFILE}
warn_days=${WARN_DAYS:-14}

check_one() {
  local url=$1 out code secs host pem expiry flag=""
  out=$(curl -s -o /dev/null --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 15 \
        -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}' "$url")
  code=${out%% *}
  secs=${out##* }
  expiry="-"
  if [[ $url == https://* ]]; then
    host=${${url#https://}%%/*}
    host=${host%%:*}
    pem=$(openssl s_client -connect "$host:443" -servername "$host" \
          < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 2>/dev/null)
    if [[ -n $pem ]]; then
      expiry=$(openssl x509 -noout -enddate <<< "$pem" | cut -d= -f2)
      openssl x509 -noout -checkend $(( warn_days * 86400 )) <<< "$pem" > /dev/null \
        || flag="  EXPIRES SOON"
    else
      expiry="no cert"
    fi
  fi
  [[ $code != 2* && $code != 3* ]] && flag="$flag  BAD STATUS"
  printf '%-34s %s %7.3fs  %s%s\n' "$url" "$code" "$secs" "$expiry" "$flag"
}

printf '%-34s %s %8s  %s\n' URL CODE TIME CERT-EXPIRES
while read -r url; do
  [[ -z $url || $url == \#* ]] && continue
  check_one "$url"
done < "$file"
chmod +x site-check.zsh && ./site-check.zsh urls.txt

$ ./site-check.zsh urls.txt
URL                                CODE     TIME  CERT-EXPIRES
http://127.0.0.1:8000/             200   0.004s  -
http://127.0.0.1:8001/status/503   503   0.003s  -  BAD STATUS
https://example.com                200   0.143s  Mar  1 23:59:59 2027 GMT
https://api.github.com             200   0.188s  Jun 27 23:59:59 2027 GMT

blocks.text: Step 4: Stretch goals

Run the checks in parallel while keeping the output sorted: have `check_one` print to a variable, collect lines with `xargs -P`, and `sort` at the end. Exit with status 1 if any site was bad so the script works in `cron` or `launchd`. Add a `--json` mode that prints the results through `jq -n`. Send yourself a notification with `osascript -e 'display notification "site down"'` when something is wrong.

It cannot run a server, but it answers `curl -I`, plain fetches and `head`/`grep` pipelines, so you can rehearse the shape of the pipelines in this chapter. Options such as `-w` and `-o` need your real Terminal, so repeat them there.

terms.def: HyperText Transfer Protocol: the text request/response protocol of the web, normally on TCP port 80
HTTP carried inside a TLS connection, normally on TCP port 443
Transport Layer Security: the protocol that encrypts a connection and authenticates the server
The first line of an HTTP request: method, target and version
The three-digit result at the start of a response; the first digit gives its class
A Name: value line that carries metadata about a request, a response or a body
A method whose repeated use has the same effect as using it once (GET, PUT, DELETE)
A 3xx response whose Location header points the client at another URL
A small value the server asks the client to store and send back; the basis of web sessions
Server Name Indication: the TLS extension that sends the wanted hostname so a server can pick its certificate
Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation: the TLS extension that agrees whether to speak HTTP/1.1 or h2
A signed document that binds a public key to a name; the server's proof of identity
Certificate authority: an organization whose signature on certificates your OS trusts
The delay until the first response byte arrives, curl's time_starttransfer
